catalog_quote: Hebrew primary stress resides within the trisyllabic window, i.e. on one of the right-most three syllables in the word, with final stress being the most common pattern (Bolozky 1982, Bat-El 1989, 1993, 2018, Graf 1999, Becker 2002, Graf and Ussishkin 2002, Cohen 2010, Pariente and Bolozky 2014, Cohen and Ussishkin 2013).
sweep_summary: Ten title hits for Modern Hebrew (hebr1245; catalog fixed-strict final, deciding source Bat-El, Cohen & Silber-Varod 2019). Newly downloaded and read: Mel'čuk & Podolsky 1996 (author's open PDF; nominal stress is morphology-controlled, stems lexically strong/weak, rightmost-morph default), Bat-El 2005 Phonology (open author PDF; most noun stems final, quite a few penultimate, a handful antepenultimate, verbs always final, noun stress must be learned per stem), Bat-El 2011/2012 segolates (open; stem-shape allomorphy, silent on the general rule), Graf 2001 ROA-443 (open precursor of Graf & Ussishkin 2003; 'lexical accent system', final = phonological default), and Churchyard 1999 abstract (Tiberian Biblical Hebrew only). Bat-El 1993 was already held by the project (scanned p. 191: 'Primary stress in Modern Hebrew nouns is distinctive'). Not obtainable: Bolozky 1982 (paywalled; abstract on rhythmic/secondary stress), Inkelas 1990 and Levin 1979/80 (print only, no online record), Hartmann et al. 2019 (paywalled sentence-prosody chapter whose Hebrew tag Glottolog itself marks as a computerized guess from 'copular'). Every first-hand source read (Bat-El 1993, 2005; Graf 2001; Mel'čuk & Podolsky 1996) confirms final as the dominant/default pattern and contradicts a strict count-based fixed: final syllable coding, matching the already-filed reclassify as fixed-dominant/lexical; none outranks the held 2019 article. all downloads were direct (author pages, OLST, ROA, the Internet Archive, Crossref/OpenAlex).

new_statements.quote: Most noun stems in Hebrew bear final stress, quite a few bear penultimate stress and there is also a handful with antepenultimate stress. As shown in Table I below, syllable structure, i.e. CV vs. CVC, does not play a role in the stress pattern, as expected in a quantity-insensitive language (Bolozky 1982, Graf 1999); both CV and CVC can be stressed on any of the last three syllables of the prosodic word. Only nouns are given here; verbs stems always bear final stress, whether the final syllable is CV (e.g. [kaná] 'he bought') or CVC (e.g. [gadál] 'he grew'). [p. 121:] Since phonological generalisations cannot be obtained, they have to learn the stress pattern of each noun stem independently
new_statements.citation: Bat-El, Outi (2005). The emergence of the trochaic foot in Hebrew hypocoristics. Phonology 22(2): 115-143.

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the leading specialist: final stress is the majority pattern in nouns and categorical in bare verb stems, but noun stress is lexically specified (final/penultimate/antepenultimate, mobile vs immobile) and not derivable from syllable count or weight; it confirms 'final = most common' and contradicts a strict fixed: final syllable coding, in line with the reclassify already filed (store B: outside the strict set as lexical, in the dominant set as fixed-dominant). Mel'čuk & Podolsky 1996:166,178 say the same in morphological terms (paradigmatic stress; rightmost morph is the unmarked default).

readall_conflicts: Prince 1975 gives a final-dominant rule for Tiberian Hebrew (final stress in consonant-final words, penultimate in a defined class of vowel-final forms), which is compatible in outline with the catalog's final-stress coding but is a different language (anci1244). The standing disagreement already held by the project for hebr1245 is untouched: Gordon's catalog record codes strict final stress, while the previously read specialist statement (Bat-El 2005, pp. 119-121; Mel'čuk & Podolsky 1996) says noun stress is lexically specified (final majority, penultimate frequent, some antepenultimate), i.e. final-dominant rather than strictly fixed: final syllable; that reclassification stands and nothing opened here bears on it.

audit.recode_to: lexical (LEX-U: lexically specified within a right-edge trisyllabic window, final most frequent — c.75% of noun stems, 68% of finite verb forms; penult in segolates, historical-guttural-final words, most loans, and C-initial-suffixed past-tense verb forms). At minimum remove from the strict set and set lexex='pervasive', for parity with Spanish/Italian/Modern Greek/Russian, which the catalog codes 'lexical'.

sources.citation: Mel'čuk, Igor & Baruch Podolsky (1996). Stress in Modern Hebrew nominal inflection. Theoretical Linguistics 22(1-2): 155-194.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 166: "According to our analysis, Modern Hebrew has thus morphology-controlled stress system. In the Hebrew grammatical tradition, stress assignment in nominals is invariably described as phonology-controlled—in terms of syllables: stress is specified as word-final (in so-called milra nominals) or penultimate (in mil'el nominals, which include segolate nouns—of the KELEV type, foreign loan words, etc.)." fn. 8: "Here is a very typical quotation: 'Stress is generally on the final syllable of the Hebrew word, less commonly on the penultimate, and rarely on the ante-penultimate' (Chayen 1973: 33)."
sources.locator: p. 166 §4.2.1 and fn. 8; p. 171 §4.2.2 stem types; p. 176; p. 178 §5.2.1 Stress Placement Rules, rule R1
sources.note: Nominal stress is 'paradigmatic', i.e. morphologically determined: every stem is lexically strong (radical stress, fixed final / prefinal / preprefinal, or 'shifting' as in dólar ~ dolár-im) or weak (suffixal stress), and suffixes are strong/weak/neutral; p. 178 rule R1 'If w does not contain dominant morphs.. then place stress on the rightmost morph. This rule is in fact the most important one in our model, since it is applied in the inflection of the majority of MH nominals: it represents the prototypical, unmarked case of stress assignment.' p. 176: 'Modern Hebrew is, of course, a rightmos…

sources.quote: 'One class of nouns is the accented class, where nouns have some lexical mark for stress ... This class includes most loan words and many native words.' sources.citation: Graf, Dafna & Adam Ussishkin (2003). Emergent iambs: Stress in Modern Hebrew. Lingua 113: 239-270. [already listed; read via the open ROA-443 precursor: Graf, Dafna (2001). Stress assignment in the nominal system of Modern Hebrew (MH). Ms., Heinrich-Heine-Universität Düsseldorf, ROA-443]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: online with a university library login (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.quote: The nominal system of MH displays a lexical accent system, where main stress assignment is a result of the interaction between lexical properties of the stem and lexical properties of the affix. In the case that no lexical properties are specified for stem and/or suffix, a general stress rule is activated, which assigns stress to the rightmost accentable syllable. In other words, final stress is the phonological "default" stress. [...] p. 2: Main stress is assigned to the final syllable (if no lexical prespecifications intervene) and secondary stress alternates rhythmically and is assigned leftwards (Bolozky 1982).
sources.locator: Abstract p. 1; §1 Introduction p. 1; §2.1 p. 2; §2.2 p. 3 (three stem groups)
sources.note: Nouns fall into Plain (final, mobile), Accented (lexically fixed) and Penultimate (segolate-type: penultimate bare, final suffixed) stems; final stress is the rhythmical default, quantity-insensitive; 'In the morphological/lexical pattern, word stress is not predictable' (p. 1).

sources.quote: §1: "The inflectional paradigms of Modern Hebrew segolates exhibit three surface stems, CVCVC, CCVC-, and CVCC-, as in dégel 'flag', dgal-ím 'flags' and digl-í 'my flag' respectively." §5.3: "The position of stress in disyllabic suffixes is determined by the properties of the final syllable: if it has an onset and a coda (CVC), it is stressed (e.g. -eyxém); otherwise, the penultimate syllable is stressed (e.g. -áix, -éynu)."
sources.locator: §1 Introduction (ms. p. 1); §2 Data and generalizations; §5.3 Possessive plural forms
sources.note: About stem-shape (syllable-structure) allomorphy in segolate paradigms, not the general stress rule; the data show penultimate stress in bare segolates (dégel) and final/suffix stress in suffixed forms (dgal-ím, digl-í), and stress placement inside disyllabic possessive suffixes.

sources.quote: In Biblical Hebrew, the tendency for rhythmic stress was primarily manifest in stress retraction, which moved word-final stress to the preceding syllable so as to avoid 'stress clash' with an immediately following word-initial stress, subject to certain restrictions. [...] In Modern Hebrew, the tendency for rhythmic stress can be realized in a variety of ways, of which stress retraction is by no means the commonest.
sources.note: About rhythmic (secondary) stress and clash resolution in Modern Hebrew, not primary-stress placement as such; cited by Bat-El 2005:119 and Graf 2001:2 for quantity-insensitivity and leftward alternating secondary stress ('Main stress is assigned to the final syllable (if no lexical prespecifications intervene) and secondary stress alternates rhythmically and is assigned leftwards (Bolozky 1982)').
